To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) insulin levels are elevated in the dietary-obes animal; and (b) insulin suppresses food ingestion in the non-obes animal.

(1) insulin elevations limit weight gain only in animals that are not insulin resistant, (2) insulin elevations reduce food intake in normal-weight animals, and (3) the mechanism by which insulin elevations limit food intake is an increase in satiety.
elevated insulin in non-obese rats limits food ingestion and meal size.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of insulin in satiety.
the role of insulin in the control of food intake and weight regulation.
the role of insulin in the regulation of feeding.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
insulin does play a role in the regulation of food intake, but that the role of this hormone is different in the obese animal.
insulin does not play an important role in the maintenance of obesity in the dietary-obes
the elevated insulin level in the obese rat is the result of insulin resistance rather than a cause.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
elevated insulin levels are associated with reduced food ingestion in the normal-weight subject, but not in the dietary-obes
insulin is elevated in obese animals and this elevated insulin is related to satiety and hypophagia.
insulin elevations limit food intake in the normal-weight animal, but do not account for the reduced food intake in the dietary-obesity model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
insulin is a potent satiety signal in the normal-weight subject.

elevated insulin does not account for the hypophagia shown by dietary-obese animals when shifted to a single diet and that elevated insulin is not the only factor accounting for the reduced food intake shown by normal-weight subjects.
the elevated insulin levels in the obese animal are not responsible for limiting food intake and, therefore, weight gain.
